display_title: US Evacuates Diplomats From Saudi Arabia
short_summary: The US State Department has ordered non-emergency staff to leave Saudi Arabia following deadly Houthi drone and missile strikes on an airport and an oil facility. The evacuation comes amid growing regional military friction and climbing oil prices.

sources.name: BBC News
sources.title: US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.title: Some US diplomats told to leave Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks

sources.name: CNBC
sources.title: U.S. pulls diplomats from Saudi Arabia as it reportedly readies Iran strikes after midterms

paragraphs: The United States Department of State has instructed non-emergency government personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia, citing an intensifying barrage of drone and missile strikes by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi movement. The ordered drawdown encompasses the American embassy in the capital, Riyadh, alongside satellite consulates throughout the kingdom. The Riyadh mission had sustained severe damage during the opening phase of the American war with Iran, operating with merely a skeleton staff for months before some diplomats recently returned.

The diplomatic evacuation followed a series of deadly strikes across Saudi territory that resulted in at least three fatalities. Saudi civil aviation authorities reported that King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, located near the Gulf coast, was struck on Wednesday evening. The assault killed one Saudi resident, injured eight people with wounds ranging from minor to serious, and caused structural damage that prompted incoming flights to divert. Simultaneously, Saudi energy authorities announced that air defenses intercepted a hostile drone targeting the Shaybah oil field near the United Arab Emirates border. Although operations remained unaffected, falling wreckage from the interception killed two people and wounded two others.

These incidents represent the latest wave in a deteriorating security environment, following an earlier strike against Riyadh’s international airport that marked the kingdom’s deadliest attack in years. In an official communication, State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott affirmed that the safety and security of American personnel remain the administration’s highest priority, warning that sustained attacks on civilian airports and vital infrastructure pose severe hazards and could escalate rapidly. Pigott also dismissed reports that Washington planned corresponding personnel withdrawals from diplomatic missions in Jordan, Bahrain, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates, clarifying that the departure directive applied exclusively to Saudi Arabia.

The escalating cross-border hostility reflects the unraveling of a fragile regional landscape. Following years of devastating conflict sparked when Houthi forces seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in 2014, an informal four-year truce had largely held. However, this tacit accord disintegrated in July when the militant faction announced a maritime embargo along the Bab al-Mandab Strait, subsequently targeting commercial tankers, energy plants, and civil transit hubs. The Houthis characterized their offensive as retaliation for an alleged Saudi blockade and a strike on Sanaa airport. Saudi Arabia has relied heavily on Red Sea transit since the conflict with Iran effectively disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Heightened diplomatic caution also unfolds against broader geopolitical friction. According to The New York Times, American and Israeli defense officials have developed operational plans for a short but intensive campaign against Iranian targets—including nuclear installations, energy infrastructure, and drone arsenals—potentially following the United States midterm elections. The report noted that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel, while fighter planes conducted strike maneuvers over Iraq. President Donald Trump has publicly stated he does not intend to resume major combat before the November election, despite previously noting interest in targeting Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility. Meanwhile, mounting tensions have rattled energy markets, propelling Brent crude past $110 per barrel and West Texas Intermediate to $98.12.

facts.fact: The US State Department ordered non-emergency government personnel and their families to leave Saudi Arabia due to escalating attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on civilian and critical infrastructure.

Three people were killed in strikes across Saudi Arabia on Wednesday evening, including one person at King Fahd International Airport in Dammam and two people from drone debris at the Shaybah oil field.
The strike at King Fahd International Airport in Dammam injured eight people, caused material damage, and prompted flights to be diverted.
Falling debris from an intercepted drone aimed at the Shaybah oil field killed two people and injured two, though oil operations were not affected.
State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott stated that the ordered departure applied only to Saudi Arabia, rejecting reports of staff withdrawals from the UAE, Jordan, Qatar, and Bahrain.

An informal four-year ceasefire between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis unravelled in July after the Houthis declared a maritime embargo in the Bab al-Mandab Strait and launched strikes on Saudi airports, tankers, and oil facilities.

The New York Times reported that US and Israeli militaries drafted plans for a short, intensive strike operation against Iran after the US midterm elections, with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth visiting Israel to meet Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Brent crude climbed above $110 per barrel amid regional disruptions.
